outcome: No progress toward the infinitude question was found since 26 January 2024: the count of known Giuga numbers (12, per OEIS A007850) has not changed since Fred Schneider's 2006 addition of a(12), no new example has been found, no bound on Giuga numbers themselves has moved, and the only 2026 documents that use the term 'Giuga number' are self-disclosed speculative/AI-generated explorations of a hypothetical Giuga number's consequences, not attempts on the infinitude question.
summary: The problem asks whether there are infinitely many Giuga numbers (composite n such that p | (n/p - 1) for every prime factor p of n; known examples are 30, 858, 1722, 66198, 2214408306, 24423128562, 432749205173838, 14737133470010574, 550843391309130318, 244197000982499715087866346, 554079914617070801288578559178, 1910667181420507984555759916338506). This is a pure existence/infinitude question, so per the scope rule (§3.1) it is only advanced by an actual resolution — not by finding one more example or narrowing a search range. I verified via OEIS A007850 that the list of known Giuga numbers is still exactly 12 terms, the same as after Fred Schneider's 2006 contribution; no new term has been added in the window and the sequence page (last touched September 2026 by routine maintenance) shows no substantive update. I initially mis-fetched OEIS A054377, which is a *different* sequence (primary pseudoperfect numbers, a related but distinct concept defined via the arithmetic derivative) and briefly appeared to show 2026 additions by 'Pedro Martins and Han M. Wang' — cross-checking against numbersaplenty.com and a fresh fetch of the correct A007850 page confirmed those 2026 additions belong to A054377, not to the Giuga numbers sequence, and are irrelevant here regardless since even a new example would not bear on infinitude. The two 2025-2026 items the triage pass surfaced are: (1) a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #2247, opened 10 Feb 2026) that only asks for a Lean *statement* of the open conjecture to be formalized — 'up for grabs', no proof attempted, formalization difficulty rated as needing only a simple predicate definition; and (2) two Zenodo preprints ('The Arithmetic Geometry of the Giuga Condition...', Sept 2025, and a related 'K-Theoretic Realization' variant) that explore hypothetical consequences if a Giuga number satisfying certain extra properties existed — the first explicitly labelled by its own authors as '[a creative exploration of a concept with AI - it should not be taken as correct mathematics]', and neither claims to settle whether Giuga numbers are finite or infinite; they only reason conditionally from a hypothetical. Wikipedia's own Giuga number article was edited in 2024 and 2026 only for formatting/citation cleanup and reorganizing the examples list, not for new mathematical content. I found no arXiv preprints, MathOverflow threads, or expert blog posts addressing the infinitude question in the window. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Zenodo 'Arithmetic Geometry of the Giuga Condition' preprints constitute 'progress' in the loose sense that they explore structural consequences of Giuga numbers using new machinery (motivic/K-theoretic). But they are explicitly conditional on a hypothetical Giuga number with extra properties, self-disclaimed as not correct mathematics (in the first case) or unreviewed and unusually speculative (in the second), and neither purports to move the infinitude question in either direction — restricting or extending the class of numbers considered is a different problem (existence of Giuga numbers with special structure), not the stated bullet, so under §3.1 this is a related/variant exploration rather than a case of the problem, and I did not code it as progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either a proof that infinitely many Giuga numbers exist (e.g. via an infinite parametrized family), a proof that only finitely many exist, or credible new terms found beyond the known 12 (which, per the existence-question scope rule, would still not settle infinitude but would at least be a search-space finding) accompanied by a peer-reviewed or widely-digested argument.
